Hip line set at your backside. Spine line through hip and neck.
Backside has left the hip line — 7% of body height toward the ball.

text.tspan: “IT MAY FEEL LIKE YOU STAY DOWN,
BUT AT IMPACT YOUR HIPS
HAVE MOVED TOWARD
THE BALL.”
Your hips moved toward the ball on the way down: 7% of
your body height between address and impact, where the
rule calls it early extension from 4%. When the hips
move in, your arms run out of room, which often shows
up as thin or blocked shots. It may feel like you stay
down, but at impact your hips have moved toward the
ball. The likely cause is restricted hip rotation:
your lead hip had turned 31° at impact, where about
45° is typical. For the rest of the bucket, do the
wall drill. At home, the 90/90 hip rotation helps the
hip turn.

svg.text: One drill and one mobility exercise from the rule table

text.tspan: Set up with your backside touching a
wall (or your golf bag). Make slow
half swings, keeping your trail glute
on the wall through impact.
Sit with both knees bent at 90°.
Rotate slowly from one side to
the other.
Generic guidance, not medical advice — see a
physiotherapist if you feel pain.

text.tspan: Answers are based only on this analysis.
No new faults, numbers or drills.
Why does it feel like I'm staying
down when I'm not?
Your chest stays over the ball, so your head
hardly moves — that is the “staying down” you
feel. The impact frame shows what your hips
did: they moved 7% of your body height toward
the ball (confidence: high), past the 4%
threshold. In the wall drill, the moment your
trail glute leaves the wall is that same
movement, so you can feel it.
Is my grip causing this?
I can't tell from this analysis — it doesn't
measure grip. What it points to is restricted
hip rotation (likely cause, confidence:
medium). For the grip, confirm with a coach.

svg.text: How do I know the drill is working?
Can I do this drill in a net?
Coach can be wrong. The measurements above are the source.
